text: The assembly will now hear an address by
his excellency Anutin Chan Viraul,
Prime Minister of the Kingdom of
Thailand. I request protocol to escort
his excellency and and invite him to
address the assembly.
Mr. President,
excellencies,
distinguished delegates,
at the outset, I congratulate you, Mr.
president on assuming
the presidency of the 81st session of
the general assembly.
It is an honor to address this assembly
for the first time as being the prime
minister of Thailand and as we mark 80
years of membership to the United
Nations.
When Thailand joined this organization,
the post-war international order was
still taking shape. Today, it is being
reshaped once again.
Many of its old certainties are giving
way. But what come next is not yet
settled. We are seeing many
transformations taking place. Power is
becoming more fragmented. Strategic
competition is becoming sharper and
international rules are under strain.
At the same time, technology is
transforming our societies while climate
change is testing our resilience.
Our institutions,
however, are struggling to keep pace.
Confidence in our ability to work
together is weakening.
And that is why this year's theme speaks
directly to the task before us. Managing
the transformation requires trust. Trust
between countries, trust in the rules we
share and trust that our institutions
can deliver.
But trust cannot be taken for granted.
It must be earned. Trust weakens when
principles are applied selectively.
When con when countries have little say
in decisions that shape their future and
when promises made in this assembly fail
to improve lives beyond it.
Rebuilding trust
means addressing each of these concerns.
We must uphold common principles
consistently.
We must give countries a genuine stake
in the international system, including a
stronger voice for the global south. And
we must take shared responsibility for
turning commitments into results.
Mr. President,
the UN's purposes remain as relevant as
ever. To promote peace and security,
human rights and dignity, sustainable
development and cooperation among
sovereign equals.
But we cannot build lasting peace if
security is assured for some and denied
to others.
Universal human rights lose their
meaning when applied selectively.
Development loses its purpose when
prosperity remains in the hands of a
few. For Thailand, peace means more than
the absence of war. It requires dialogue
to settle differences and respect for
international law so that all countries
can live with security and dignity.
The situation in Palestine continues to
demand our attention. It reminds us that
the principles we uphold
must protect people when they need them
the most. That is why human must be
human rights must be universal in
practice. As a member of human rights
council, Thailand believes that our work
must reach beyond resolutions and make a
real difference in people's lives.
Development must be people centered and
sustainable. Growth must improve
people's lives today without closing off
the opportunities of tomorrow.
Consistent application of principles
gives countries the confidence that they
will be treated fairly. But that
confidence must also extend to how
decisions are made. Countries need to
know that their voices count. Mr.
President, the UN's membership has
become nearly universal, but
representation has not evolved at the
same pace.
An international system cannot command
trust if large parts of its membership
feel they have too little to say in
shaping it. Rebuilding trust requires
shared ownership.
The United Nations must reflect today's
world, not the distribution of power 80
years ago. And that is why Thailand
supports security council reform that
gives developing countries and
underrepresented regions particularly in
the global south a greater role in
decision making. Asia too must be better
represented for all its economic weight.
Asia must be able to help shape global
decisions and carry more responsibility
for the outcomes
and representation must also mean that
women have a meaningful voice in the
decisions that shape our common future.
They are already at the forefront of
this organization's work from
development to peacekeeping.
As the UN considers its next secretary
general, maybe it is time that this
representation be reflected at the
highest level. Representation and
effectiveness must advance together. We
commend Mr. Secretary General Antonio
Gutirez for his commitment to reform
including through the UN80 initiative.
We stand ready to work with his
successor to carry this work forward.
Mr. President, having a stronger voice
in global institutions mean countries
working together on the problems
closest to them. This is where regional
cooperation has a vital role. The United
Nations must remain the centerpiece of
the mult multilateral system. But we
cannot expect it to do everything. It
cannot settle problems when member
states are not willing to act. Regional
institutions can help turn that
willingness into cooperation. They bring
countries together around
shared challenges and translate global
principles suited to local
realities.
In this way, regionalism
becomes a building block of effective
multilateralism.
ASEAN has demonstrated this for almost
six decades. It has grown from five to
11 member states. We do not always
agree, but we have learned to manage
differences and preserve space for
cooperation.
For my country, Thailand, that practical
cooperation means serving as a trusted
platform. We want to leverage our
strengths as a logistical hub and
manufacturing base to connect markets
and supply chains across our region. Our
conviction is that together we should
combine Asia's diversity for
co-creation,
bringing together the different
strengths of our countries to promote
chat prosperity.
The same thinking should also extend
beyond Asia.
Thailand continues to pursue free trade
agreements with partners across region
and to expand trade and opportunities
for both sides. Additionally, our
Thailand Africa initiative seeks to
deepen political, economic and
development cooperation to build
partnerships of equals across our
regions.

institution earn trust through what
their members are prepared to do. A
greater voice must come with a
willingness to contribute.
Shared ownership therefore must lead to
shared responsibility.
The shadow begins with the words we the
peoples. Thailand believes that this
work must begin at home.
The SDG
sustainable development goals provide us
with an important framework that goes
beyond development. Ultimately, they are
about enabling people to live in peace
and dignity. Progress towards achieving
the SDGs also shapes how we are building
a strong and resilient economy and how
we remain accountable to our people.
Thailand will leverage our strengths. We
are building upon our strong
agricultural base to be a source of food
security for the world. Meanwhile, our
universal health coverage ensures that
people have access to affordable and
quality health care while also
developing Thailand into a medical and
wellness hub. Additionally,
our energy transition efforts take
Thailand closer to meeting climate
obligations. And through our solar
rooftop policy, we are also creating
greater economic opportunities for
households by allowing them to sell
excess electricity back to the grid.
However, this responsibility goes beyond
development.
Thailand's humanitarian tradition
demonstrates this conviction. In the
late 70s, we provided temporary refuge
and assist assistance to large numbers
of Cambodians fleeing violence and
famine. Today we are giving displaced
persons from Myanmar who have lived in
the temporary shelters in Thailand for
decades greater opportunities to work
and support their families.
For the Rohingya transiting in Thailand,
we have adopted a community-based
alternative to immigration detention for
Rohingya children to better protect
their rights and access to services. Our
our responsibility as a neighbor also
means addressing the challenges in our
own neighborhood. One of those
challenges is the dispute between our
country and our neighbor being Cambodia.
We have been through difficult period.
When I met with Prime Minister Hun Manet
in May, we sought to resolve difficult
issues through bilateral dialogue where
rebuilding trust and confidence in order
to move forward together. It is
regrettable that Cambodia did not give
dialogue a genuine chance and chose a
different path by initiating compulsory
consiliation proceedings under UNL.
Nevertheless,
Thailand is engaging in good faith, but
our position is clear. This process
concerns the delimitation of maritime
boundaries only.
In the meantime,
Cambodia must work with us to strengthen
security along our shared border,
including through concrete cooperation
to combat online scams and demining,
sorry, demining.
Our communities will not be safe if we
do not make concrete progress on these
matters.
Ultimately, our shared border must be a
place of shared prosperity, not one that
continues to bear the scars of conflict.
Let me be clear, Thailand has never
sought conflict. But peace can only be
built when we work together in earnest.
And surely this will require genuine
effort from our neighbor Cambodia. That
same commitment guides our approach to
Myanmar.
Thailand supports peace, national
reconciliation, and a durable solution
that is Myanmar late and Myanmar own. We
believe in constructive and calibrated
re-engagement within ASEAN and in
coordination with relevant partners
while encouraging concrete pro concrete
progress on the ground. In both cases,
our responsibility is to make dialogue
possible and progress achievable.
And when threats cross borders,
responsibility must be shared more
widely.
My country has stepped up efforts on
prevention and suppression of narcotics
through our partnership with the UN ODC,
other regional and international
organization as well as neighboring
countries and through the global
partnership against online scams,
Thailand is bringing all the relevant
stakeholders together to prevent these
crimes.
Mr. President, 80 years ago in our first
address to this assembly, the Kingdom of
Siam affirmed that it followed the path
of peaceful settlement
and friendly cooperation.
That path still guides Thailand today.
As a new international order takes
shape, we must carry that spirit
forward. No country can write its future
alone and no international order can
earn lasting trust if too many countries
feel that the system is written for them
but not with them. A rulebased
international order with share ownership
in shaping our common future is the
condition that will help rebuild that
trust.
The future of United Nations will depend
on the trust we rebuild through our
action today. And let us give every
nation reason to believe in the new in
the United Nations and every person
reason to believe that the United
Nations can deliver for them. Thank you
very much.
On behalf of the assembly,
I wish to thank the prime minister of
the Kingdom of Thailand.
